aliases: The standardization of the Qur'an under Uthman
Jam' al-Qur'an (the collection of the Qur'an)

location: Medina, with copies sent to the provinces of the caliphate

date.note: The traditional account places the standardization in the caliphate of Uthman (23-35/644-656). The campaign during which Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman reportedly raised the alarm is identified by Nicolai Sinai, following Noldeke and Schwally, with a campaign of 30/650-1; M. M. al-Azami, following Ibn Hajar, adopts 25/645-6 and notes that the reports give dates ranging from 25 to 30 AH. The earlier collection under Abu Bakr is placed in his caliphate (11-13/632-634), after the Battle of al-Yamama. The year given is approximate.

summary: The Uthmanic Codex is the standard written text (mushaf) of the Qur'an that Islamic tradition credits to the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, who around 650 CE (c. 25-30 AH) is reported to have had copies made from an earlier collection and sent to the provinces. The traditional account, its historical reliability, and the date at which the Qur'an's consonantal text became fixed are the subject of long-running scholarly debate.
description:
The best-known account of how the Qur'an came to exist as a single written codex is carried by two reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the chapter on the collection of the Qur'an in the Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an, both transmitted through Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri (d. 124/741-2). In the first (no. 4986), Zayd ibn Thabit relates that after heavy casualties among those who knew the Qur'an by heart (the qurra') at the Battle of al-Yamama, Umar urged the caliph Abu Bakr to have the Qur'an collected, fearing that much of it might be lost. Abu Bakr at first asked, 'How can you do something which Allah's Apostle did not do?', and then charged Zayd, who had written down revelation for the Prophet, with the task. Zayd reports collecting it 'from palm stalks, thin white stones and also from the men who knew it by heart', and says that the complete manuscript remained with Abu Bakr until his death, then with Umar, and then with Umar's daughter Hafsa. In the second report (no. 4987), Anas ibn Malik relates that Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, alarmed by differences in recitation between the troops of Syria and Iraq campaigning in Armenia and Azerbaijan, urged Uthman to 'save this nation before they differ about the Book as Jews and the Christians did before'. Uthman obtained Hafsa's manuscripts and ordered Zayd ibn Thabit, Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn al-As, and Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham to copy them, instructing the three Qurashi members to write in the dialect of Quraysh where they differed from Zayd, 'as the Qur'an was revealed in their tongue'. He then sent a copy to every province and ordered all other Qur'anic material, 'whether written in fragmentary manuscripts or whole copies', to be burnt. Classical sources also transmit other reports; Sinai notes that the tradition is not unanimous on who first collected the Qur'an, and al-Azami records a second, less well-known narration in which Uthman first had an independent copy compiled by a committee of twelve from primary written materials before comparing it with Hafsa's sheets (suhuf).

In Muslim doctrine the Qur'an is held to be divinely preserved, a belief grounded in verses such as Q 15:9: 'It is certainly We Who have revealed the Reminder, and it is certainly We Who will preserve it.' The contemporary Muslim scholar M. M. al-Azami presents this position historically: on his account the Qur'an had been written down in its entirety during the Prophet's lifetime but not bound into one volume; Abu Bakr's collection gathered it into sheets; and Uthman's work produced uniform copies to end disputes over recitation, with Hafsa's sheets playing a critical role in both narrations of his method.

Modern academic scholarship has long debated how far the traditional account can be relied on and when the consonantal skeleton (rasm) of the Qur'an reached closure. As Sinai summarizes the debate, Paul Casanova and Alphonse Mingana early in the twentieth century attributed the codification to the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik (r. 685-705) and his governor al-Hajjaj, while Friedrich Schwally's revision of Noldeke's history accepted an Uthmanic origin, which became the default view. In 1977 John Wansbrough's Quranic Studies argued, on form-critical and literary grounds, for a much later canonization, placing the closure of the text toward the end of the eighth century. In his own words, since early Muslim jurisprudence was, with few exceptions, not derived from the Qur'an and the literary activity of stabilizing the text is not attested before the third/ninth century, 'establishment of a standard text such as is implied by the 'Uthmanic recension traditions can hardly have been earlier.' Sinai reports that this very late dating has increasingly come to be seen as untenable, while a number of scholars (among them Chase Robinson, Alfred-Louis de Premare, David Powers, and Stephen Shoemaker) have favoured codification or significant revision under Abd al-Malik. Harald Motzki's analysis of the chains of transmission (isnad) traced the reports about the Abu Bakr and Uthman collections back at least to al-Zuhri, earlier than some previous critics had assumed; Sinai notes that this result does not by itself exclude the later-codification hypothesis. Sinai also cautions that, even granting an Uthmanic standardization, the surrounding details (Hudhayfa's role, the motive, and whether the text was a faithful copy of Hafsa's sheets) cannot be reliably ascertained, noting that al-Zuhri, the common link of the reports, may legitimately be suspected, following Goldziher, of having been susceptible to Umayyad 'state expediency'.

Manuscript evidence has become central to the debate. The lower, erased text of the Sana'a palimpsest (Sana'a 1), edited by Behnam Sadeghi and Mohsen Goudarzi, is recognizably a version of the Qur'an but diverges from the standard rasm in wording and sura order; Sadeghi and Goudarzi treat it as the only known material witness to a non-standard recension. As reported by Sinai, radiocarbon dating of a folio associated with it, published by Sadeghi and Uwe Bergmann, gave a 95 per cent probability that the parchment dates between 578 and 669 CE. Francois Deroche's study of Umayyad-period Qur'an manuscripts stresses the continuing development of copying and orthographic practice under the Umayyads and cautions about the limits of radiocarbon dating. Alba Fedeli's codicological work showed that two leaves in Birmingham's Mingana collection (Islamic Arabic 1572a), written in the early Hijazi script, belong to the same codex as leaves held in Paris. Weighing the literary and manuscript evidence, Sinai concludes that, unless Qur'anic passages with a distinct profile are convincingly placed in the late seventh century, the traditional dating of the standard rasm (excepting certain orthographic features) to 650 or earlier 'ought to be our default view'. The question remains debated.
editorial_notes:
This entry separates three things: the traditional account, reported in the words of the canonical hadith; the Muslim doctrinal position on the Qur'an's preservation, stated as an attributed belief and not as fact endorsed or disputed by the editor (neutrality #1, #4); and the modern academic debate, in which each position is attributed to named scholars and none is declared correct (neutrality #2). Sinai's conclusion is reported as his conclusion, and the editor does not adjudicate between the positions in the modern debate. The late-canonization thesis is presented chiefly through Sinai's survey, supplemented by one directly read passage from Wansbrough himself, and attributed to Wansbrough and the others Sinai names, and the traditional and Muslim-scholarly positions are given in their own terms. The related_to link to tahrif records a thematic relation between two doctrines about how scripture is transmitted (the Qur'an's preservation and the charge that earlier scriptures were altered), made explicit in the hadith by Hudhayfa's reference to Jews and Christians; it makes no judgment on either doctrine or on any community's scripture.

The Birmingham claim is limited to Fedeli's codicological identification; the separately reported radiocarbon result for the Birmingham leaves is not stated because no scholarly publication of it was read.

Sourcing triangulates the three lenses per neutrality #8: (a) Western academic scholarship (Sinai, Motzki, Wansbrough, Deroche, Sadeghi and Goudarzi, Fedeli); (b) classical primary texts (Sahih al-Bukhari; the Qur'an); (c) a modern Muslim scholar (al-Azami). No encyclopedias or tertiary sources are cited (neutrality #9). Dates are given in hijri and CE.

relations.note: In the traditional account the caliph Uthman ordered Hafsa's manuscripts to be copied into uniform codices, sent a copy to each province, and ordered other written Qur'anic material to be burnt (Sahih al-Bukhari 4987).
In the traditional account the Uthmanic copies were made from sheets first collected by Zayd ibn Thabit at Abu Bakr's command after the Battle of al-Yamama (Sahih al-Bukhari 4986).

In the traditional account Umar urged Abu Bakr to have the Qur'an collected after the losses at al-Yamama, and the collected sheets passed into his keeping and then to his daughter Hafsa (Sahih al-Bukhari 4986).
Both the Abu Bakr collection and the Uthmanic standardization are placed by the tradition in the period of the first caliphs (11-35/632-656).
Sahih al-Bukhari transmits the two best-known reports of the Qur'an's collection (nos. 4986 and 4987, in the Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an), both through al-Zuhri.

Thematic relation between two doctrines about how scripture is transmitted: Muslim doctrine holds the Qur'an to be preserved, while tahrif concerns the charge that earlier scriptures were altered. In the hadith account, Hudhayfa urges Uthman to act before the community differs about its Book 'as Jews and the Christians did before'. The link reports this relation and makes no judgment on either doctrine.

Compares the question, not the answer, per neutrality principle #10. Both traditions claim an authoritative scriptural text and give accounts of how that text came to be fixed. The difference: the Islamic account centres on a caliphal standardization of the wording of a single corpus within about two decades of Muhammad's death, with modern scholars debating when the consonantal text reached closure; the New Testament canon concerns which of many existing writings were recognized as scripture, a gradual process over roughly the second to fourth centuries. This link ranks neither tradition and treats neither as the measure of the other.
